93499.q: What can you see well on your fingertip with a magnifying glass?
93499.e: Everyone has fine lines on their fingertips. These ridges make the fingerprint.
93499.m: With a magnifying glass you can see the ridges of your fingerprint.

93500.q: Why do many people wear glasses?
93500.e: If the eyes don't see sharply, glasses help. Their lenses guide the light into the eye correctly.

93501.q: Where do you usually get new glasses?
93501.e: The optician measures your eyes and fits the glasses. For eye problems, the eye doctor can help too.
93501.m: You get glasses at the optician's.

93502.q: What do sunglasses protect your eyes from?
93502.e: Good sunglasses block glaring light and harmful UV rays. That protects the eyes.
93502.m: Sunglasses protect your eyes from glaring light.

93503.q: What does a short-sighted person see blurrily without glasses?
93503.e: Short-sighted people see close things sharply. What is far away, like the board at school, they see blurrily.
93503.m: Short-sighted people see blurrily in the distance.

93504.q: What can you put directly on your eye instead of wearing glasses?
93504.e: Contact lenses are small, thin shells. They sit directly on the eye and work like the lenses in glasses.

93505.q: What do many older people need reading glasses for?
a: To read small print close up
93505.e: As people get older, their eyes find it harder to focus on close things. Reading glasses help with reading.
93505.m: Older people often need reading glasses.

93506.q: Which glasses protect you from snow and wind when skiing?
93506.e: Ski goggles fit closely around the eyes. They protect from wind, snow and glaring light.
93506.m: When skiing, ski goggles protect your eyes.

93507.q: In which country were the first glasses made over 700 years ago?
93507.e: The first glasses appeared around 1300 in northern Italy. They didn't have arms yet and just sat on the nose.
93507.m: The first glasses came from Italy.

93508.q: What are the parts of a pair of glasses that rest over the ears called?
93508.e: The arms hold the glasses in place behind the ears. The bridge rests on the nose.
93508.m: The arms of glasses rest over the ears.

93510.q: In which vehicle do people use a periscope to look above the water?
93510.e: A submarine dives under water. With the periscope, the crew looks above the surface of the water.
93510.m: In a submarine you look up out of the water with the periscope.

93511.q: How many mirrors does a simple periscope need?
93511.e: At the top, one mirror directs the light down into the tube. At the bottom, a second mirror directs it into the eye.
93511.m: A simple periscope has two mirrors.

93512.q: What can you use a periscope for on land?
93512.e: With a periscope you can see over obstacles without climbing over them yourself.
93512.m: With a periscope you can see over a wall.

93513.q: How are the two mirrors placed in a simple periscope?
93513.e: Both mirrors are fitted at an angle. That way they direct the light round the corner into the tube and out again.
93513.m: The mirrors in a periscope are fitted at an angle.

93514.q: What can you use to make a simple periscope yourself?
93514.e: You can take an empty milk carton, for example. At the top and bottom you glue in a small mirror at an angle.
93514.m: You can make a periscope from cardboard and two mirrors.

93515.q: Which way up is the picture in a simple periscope with two mirrors?
93515.e: The first mirror turns the picture, the second turns it back. So you see everything upright.
93515.m: In a periscope you see the picture upright.

93516.q: What does the word “periscope” roughly mean?
93516.e: The word comes from Greek. “Peri” means around and “skopein” means to look.

93517.q: What do you see when you look into a kaleidoscope?
93517.e: In a kaleidoscope, colourful, regular patterns appear. They often look like a star.
93517.m: In a kaleidoscope you see colourful patterns.

93518.e: Strips of mirror are fitted inside the tube. At the end there are colourful pieces of glass or beads.
93518.m: A kaleidoscope contains mirrors and colourful pieces.

93519.q: What happens when you turn a kaleidoscope?
93519.e: When you turn it, the colourful pieces tumble about. The mirrors immediately make a new pattern from them.
93519.m: Turning a kaleidoscope makes a new pattern.

93520.q: What are the patterns in a kaleidoscope like?
a: All jumbled up with no order
93520.e: The mirrors repeat the colourful pieces several times. That is why the patterns are regular, like a star or a flower.
93520.m: The mirrors make regular patterns in a kaleidoscope.

93521.q: About how many years ago was the kaleidoscope invented?
93521.e: The Scotsman David Brewster invented the kaleidoscope in 1816. That is about 200 years ago.
93521.m: The kaleidoscope was invented about 200 years ago.

93522.q: What does the word “kaleidoscope” roughly mean?
93522.e: The word comes from Greek. It roughly means “seeing beautiful shapes”.

93523.q: How often do you see exactly the same pattern again in a kaleidoscope?
93523.e: The pieces fall differently by chance every time. That is why exactly the same pattern almost never appears twice.
93523.m: In a kaleidoscope, a pattern almost never repeats.

93524.q: Where is it best to point a kaleidoscope when you look into it?
93524.e: The colourful pieces only light up when light shines through them. That is why you hold the kaleidoscope up to a window or a lamp.
93524.m: You hold a kaleidoscope up to the light.

93525.e: In a mirror maze there are very many mirrors. You often have to search for the way through.
93525.m: A mirror maze is a room full of mirrors.

93526.q: Where in Switzerland do you often find a mirror maze?
93526.e: At the Chilbi, the funfair, there are often mirror mazes. You can get lost there between the mirrors.
93526.m: At the Chilbi there is often a mirror maze.

93527.q: In which Swiss city is there a famous mirror maze in the Glacier Garden?
93527.e: In the Glacier Garden in Lucerne there is the mirror maze “Alhambra”. It is over 100 years old.
93527.m: In the Glacier Garden in Lucerne there is a mirror maze.

93528.q: Why is it easy to get lost in a mirror maze?
a: You don't know what is real
93528.e: The mirrors show lots of passages that don't really exist. You don't know where a real path is.
93528.m: In a mirror maze you see lots of false passages.

93529.q: What do you see if you stand between two mirrors hanging exactly opposite each other?
a: Lots of reflections one behind the other
93529.e: The mirrors reflect each other again and again. That makes a long row of reflections.
93529.m: Two mirrors facing each other show lots of reflections.

93530.q: What helps you not to walk into a mirror in a mirror maze?
a: Stretching your hands out in front
93530.e: With your hands stretched out, you feel the mirror before you bump into it with your head.
93530.m: In a mirror maze you stretch your hands out in front.

93531.q: In which famous palace in France is there a large Hall of Mirrors?
93531.e: In the Palace of Versailles near Paris there is the Hall of Mirrors. Hundreds of mirrors hang on its walls.
93531.m: The Palace of Versailles has a famous Hall of Mirrors.

93532.q: How does your reflection look on the inside of a shiny spoon?
93532.e: The inside of the spoon curves inwards. If you look into it from a little further away, your picture is upside down.
93532.m: In the bowl of a spoon you are upside down.

93533.q: How do you look on the back of a shiny spoon?
93533.e: The back of the spoon curves outwards. In it, your picture is upright but smaller.
93533.m: On the back of a spoon you are upright and small.

93534.q: What do you call a mirror that curves inwards like the inside of a spoon?
93534.e: A mirror that curves inwards is called a concave mirror. The bowl of a spoon is a small concave mirror.
93534.m: The inside of a spoon is a concave mirror.

93535.q: What do you call a mirror that curves outwards like the back of a spoon?
93535.e: A mirror that curves outwards is called a convex mirror. It shows everything smaller, but a large area.
93535.m: The back of a spoon is a convex mirror.

93536.q: Why is your reflection in a spoon distorted?
a: Because the spoon is made of wood
93536.e: A spoon is not flat but bent. Bent mirrors distort the picture.
93536.m: A spoon distorts the picture because it is curved.

93537.e: A metal spoon that is polished smooth and shiny reflects light well. Wood and scratches scatter the light.
93537.m: A shiny metal spoon reflects well.

93538.q: How is the Olympic flame lit at Olympia in Greece?
a: With sunlight and a concave mirror
With an oil lamp from a temple
93538.e: At Olympia, a concave mirror focuses sunlight on one point. It gets so hot there that the torch catches fire.
93538.m: The Olympic flame is lit with a concave mirror.

93539.q: What is behind the bulb of a torch so that the light shines forwards?
93539.e: Behind the bulb there is a shiny concave mirror. It collects the light and sends it forwards.
93539.m: A concave mirror directs a torch's light forwards.

93540.q: Which instrument lets you look at tiny things like cells very greatly magnified?
93540.e: A microscope magnifies much more strongly than a magnifying glass. With it you can even see tiny cells.

93541.q: What lets you see faraway animals in the forest closer?
93541.e: Binoculars seem to bring faraway things closer.
93541.m: With binoculars you see faraway things closer.

93542.q: A magnifying glass magnifies 3 times. How long does a 2 cm beetle look through it?
93542.e: 3 times means three times as big. So 2 cm times 3 equals 6 cm.
93542.m: With 3 times magnification, everything looks three times as big.

93543.e: With 10 times magnification, a thing looks ten times as big as it really is.
93543.m: 10 times means ten times as big.

93544.q: What do stargazers use to look at the Moon magnified?
93544.e: A telescope is a large instrument for looking at faraway things. With it you can see craters on the Moon and distant planets.
93544.m: With a telescope you see the Moon magnified.

93545.q: Which mirror in the bathroom shows your face magnified?
93545.e: A make-up mirror curves slightly inwards. If you look into it close up, your face looks bigger.
93545.m: A make-up mirror magnifies your face.

93546.q: Does an ant really get bigger when you look at it through a magnifying glass?
a: Yes, when the sun is shining
93546.e: The magnifying glass only bends the light differently. The ant itself stays exactly the same size.
93546.m: A magnifying glass doesn't really make things bigger.

93547.q: A pencil is 1 cm thick and looks 4 cm thick through a magnifying glass. How many times does the glass magnify?
93547.e: 1 cm becomes 4 cm. 4 divided by 1 is 4, so the glass magnifies 4 times.
93547.m: The magnification tells you how many times bigger something looks.

93548.q: What happens to your picture in the bowl of a spoon when you get very close?
a: It is upright and becomes big
It stays upside down and tiny
93548.e: Very close to a concave mirror, the picture turns round. It is then upright and magnified.
93548.m: Very close to the spoon, you see yourself upright and big.

93549.q: What does your reflection look like on a soap bubble?
93549.e: A soap bubble is round and shiny. Like a funhouse mirror, it shows you small and distorted.
93549.m: A soap bubble shows you small and distorted.

93550.q: Which country built the GPS satellite navigation system and operates it?
93550.e: GPS was developed by the US Department of Defense. Today it is operated by the US Space Force and used all over the world.
93550.m: GPS is a navigation system of the USA.

93551.q: From at least how many satellites does a GPS receiver need signals to work out its position and altitude accurately?
93551.e: Three satellites would be enough for the position if the clock in the receiver were perfect. The fourth satellite makes up for the error of the receiver’s clock.
93551.m: For an accurate position, GPS needs at least four satellites.

93552.q: Why are China and Europe building their own navigation systems, even though GPS exists?
a: They do not want to depend on the USA
GPS does not work outside the USA
Their mobile phones do not understand GPS
93552.e: GPS belongs to the USA, which could restrict it in an emergency. That is why China has built its own system, BeiDou, and Europe has built Galileo.
93552.m: Their own navigation systems make countries independent of GPS.

93553.q: Which device on board GPS satellites is especially important for working out positions?
93553.e: The receiver calculates the distance to each satellite from the travel time of the signals. This needs extremely accurate atomic clocks.
93553.m: Atomic clocks make GPS positioning accurate.

93554.q: What is the name of the European satellite navigation system that Switzerland also takes part in?
93554.e: Galileo is the navigation system of the European Union. Switzerland takes part in it through an agreement with the EU.
93554.m: Galileo is the European counterpart to GPS.

93555.q: What does a GPS receiver actually measure to calculate its distance from a satellite?
a: The travel time of the radio signal
93555.e: Radio signals travel at the speed of light. The distance follows from the time the signal takes.
93555.m: GPS calculates distances from the travel time of radio signals.

93556.q: What can a device with GPS work out?
93556.e: A GPS receiver uses the signals from several satellites to calculate where it is. The system has been fully working since 1995.
93556.m: With GPS you work out your location.

93557.q: What do the pictures from weather satellites mainly show?
a: Clouds and weather systems from above
The roads with all the cars
93557.e: Weather satellites photograph the Earth from above. Their pictures show where clouds, fronts and storms are.
93557.m: Weather satellites show the clouds from above.

93558.q: What are the European weather satellites called whose pictures MeteoSwiss also uses?
93558.e: Meteosat satellites are operated by the organisation EUMETSAT. Switzerland is a member and uses the data for weather forecasts.
93558.m: MeteoSwiss uses pictures from the Meteosat satellites.

93559.q: At what height above the equator are geostationary weather satellites like Meteosat?
93559.e: At about 36,000 km, one orbit takes exactly as long as one turn of the Earth. The satellite then seems to stand still above one point.
93559.m: Geostationary satellites are at a height of about 36,000 km.

93560.q: Why can weather satellites take pictures of clouds at night too?
93560.e: Clouds, land and sea give off heat radiation. Infrared cameras measure this radiation even without sunlight.
93560.m: With infrared, weather satellites can see clouds at night too.

93561.q: What advantage do weather satellites in a polar orbit have?
a: Bit by bit they fly over the whole Earth
They fly more than 1 million km away
93561.e: Polar satellites orbit over the poles at a height of about 800 km. Because the Earth turns beneath them, they see the whole Earth over time.
93561.m: Satellites in polar orbits observe the whole Earth.

93562.q: Which dangerous weather events over the sea can be spotted early thanks to weather satellites?
93562.e: Tropical storms form over warm seas, where there are hardly any measuring stations. Satellite pictures show their cloud spirals early.

93563.q: Which organisation based in Darmstadt operates the European weather satellites?
93563.e: EUMETSAT is the European organisation for weather satellites. Switzerland is one of its member states.
93563.m: EUMETSAT operates the European weather satellites.

93564.q: Why do geostationary weather satellites only see the polar regions badly?
93564.e: Geostationary satellites are high above the equator. They only see the polar regions at a very steep slant at the edge of the picture.
93564.m: From above the equator, a satellite sees the poles only badly.

93566.q: Roughly how long does a signal take from the Earth to a geostationary satellite 36,000 km up and back?
93566.e: Radio travels at about 300,000 km per second. 72,000 km divided by 300,000 km/s makes about 0.24 seconds.
93566.m: Signals via geostationary satellites have a short delay.

93649.q: Roughly when did the Goldau landslide happen?
93649.e: On 2 September 1806, a huge mass of rock crashed into the valley. That is about 200 years ago.

93650.q: Which mountain did the Goldau landslide break away from?
93650.e: The mass of rock broke away from the southern side of the Rossberg below the Gnipenspitze. Opposite is the Rigi, up which the masses surged.
93650.m: The Goldau landslide came from the Rossberg.

93651.q: Roughly how many people died in the Goldau landslide?
93651.e: 457 people died in the landslide. More than 300 animals were also killed.
93651.m: 457 people died in the Goldau landslide.

93652.q: In which canton is Goldau, which became known for a huge landslide?
93652.e: Goldau belongs to the municipality of Arth in the canton of Schwyz. The village lies between Lake Zug and Lake Lauerz.
93652.m: Goldau is in the canton of Schwyz.

93653.q: Which rock was the mass of the Goldau landslide mainly made of?
93653.e: The mountain consists of sloping layers of cemented gravel, called Nagelfluh. This rock is very common in the foothills of the Alps.
93653.m: At Goldau, mainly Nagelfluh crashed into the valley.

93654.q: What made the slope of the Rossberg slippery before the Goldau landslide?
a: Lots of rain softened layers of rock
93654.e: Rainwater got in through cracks and softened clay-rich marl layers. The slabs of rock slid off on them like on a slide.
93654.m: At Goldau, softened rock layers became a slide.

93655.q: Which lake was partly buried by the Goldau landslide, causing a flood wave?
93655.e: Part of the mass of rock went into Lake Lauerz, which became about a seventh smaller as a result. Eyewitnesses reported a flood wave about 20 metres high.
93655.m: The Goldau landslide made Lake Lauerz smaller.

93656.q: What is there today between the big boulders of the Goldau landslide area?
93656.e: The Goldau Nature and Animal Park lies in the middle of the debris field of the landslide. The boulders still shape the landscape today.
93656.m: Today there is an animal park in the Goldau landslide area.

93657.q: Roughly how much rock crashed into the valley in the Goldau landslide?
93657.e: Experts estimate the mass at almost 40 million cubic metres. It buried an area of about 6.5 square kilometres.
93657.m: At Goldau, almost 40 million cubic metres of rock came down.

93658.q: In which canton is Elm, which became known for a devastating landslide?
93658.e: Elm lies at the far end of the Sernf valley in the canton of Glarus. Today it belongs to the municipality of Glarus Süd.
93658.m: Elm is in the Sernf valley in Glarus.

93659.q: Roughly when did the Elm landslide happen?
93659.e: On 11 September 1881, a huge mass of rock fell from the Plattenbergkopf onto the village of Elm. That is about 150 years ago.

93660.q: Which human activity contributed greatly to the Elm landslide?
93660.e: For years slate was quarried on the slope, which hollowed out the mountain. Together with heavy rain, the slope lost its hold.
93660.m: Slate quarrying made the slope near Elm unstable.

93661.q: Roughly how many people died in the Elm landslide?
93661.e: 114 people died in the landslide. In addition, 83 buildings were destroyed.
93661.m: More than 100 people died in the Elm landslide.

93662.q: What was the rock quarried at Elm once used for, among other things?
93662.e: The rock can be split into thin slabs. Among other things, it was used to make slates and slate pencils for schoolchildren.
93662.m: The rock from Elm used to be made into writing slates.

93663.q: Which experts study landslides like the one at Elm?
93663.e: Geologists study rock and mountains. The Elm landslide was studied, for example, by the well-known geologist Albert Heim.

93664.q: Roughly how much rock came down in the Elm landslide?
93664.e: About 10 million cubic metres of rock broke away from the Plattenbergkopf. This mass buried a large part of the village.
93664.m: At Elm, about 10 million cubic metres of rock came down.

93665.q: How did the Elm landslide happen?
a: Two smaller falls were followed by the main fall
Everything came down in one second
The slope slid slowly over weeks
An earthquake blew the summit away
93665.e: First two smaller falls came down, which attracted curious onlookers. Shortly afterwards came the main fall, which hit many of these people.
93665.m: At Elm, three rockfalls came one after another.

93666.q: What is the difference between a rockfall and a rock avalanche?
a: In a rock avalanche, much more rock comes down
A rock avalanche only happens in winter
A rockfall is made only of ice
93666.e: Rockfalls are smaller. With huge masses of over a million cubic metres, as at Goldau, it is called a rock avalanche.
93666.m: A rock avalanche is much bigger than a rockfall.

93667.q: What often triggers a debris flow?
93667.e: Heavy rain or fast snowmelt soaks loose material in steep gullies. This then suddenly starts to move.
93667.m: Heavy rain can trigger debris flows.

93668.q: Where are the biggest boulders in a debris flow usually found?
a: At the front of the debris flow
Right at the end of the debris flow
Only at the bottom under the mud
93668.e: The big boulders collect at the front, in the so-called head of the flow. This front is especially destructive.
93668.m: The head at the front carries the biggest boulders.

93669.q: Why do scientists measure debris flows in the Illgraben in Valais every year?
a: To understand debris flows better and warn about them
To find gold in the debris
To use the stream for a reservoir
93669.e: The Illgraben near Leuk is one of the most active debris flow streams in the Alps. Instruments record several debris flows there every year so that they can be better understood.
93669.m: Debris flows are measured in the Illgraben in Valais.

93670.q: Which village in the Grisons was hit by debris flows in 2017 after a landslide on Piz Cengalo?
93670.e: In August 2017, about three million cubic metres of rock fell from Piz Cengalo. This led to debris flows that reached the village of Bondo in the Bregaglia.
93670.m: In 2017, debris flows reached the village of Bondo in the Bregaglia.

93671.q: Which change in the high mountains can make debris flows more frequent because of climate change?
93671.e: When permanently frozen ground thaws, a lot of loose material is set free. In heavy rain it can flow away as a debris flow.
93671.m: Thawing permafrost provides material for debris flows.

93672.q: Why are debris flows much more dangerous than an ordinary flood?
a: They carry heavy stones and mud
They consist only of clear water
93672.e: A debris flow is much denser and heavier than water alone. It can destroy houses, bridges and roads and bury everything under debris.
93672.m: Debris flows destroy things because of their heavy load.

93673.q: What is the fan-shaped pile of debris called that debris flows leave at the mouth of a mountain stream?
93673.e: Where the mountain stream comes out into the flatter valley, the material is left behind. Over a long time this forms an alluvial fan, on which villages often stand.
93673.m: Debris flows leave debris on alluvial fans.

93676.q: What is a debris basin on a debris flow stream for?
93676.e: A debris basin is a big basin with a grid or dam. It holds back the rock carried along before it reaches villages.
93676.m: Debris basins hold back debris from debris flows.

93677.q: Which river's catchment area do all of Liechtenstein's debris flow streams belong to?
93677.e: Liechtenstein lies on the Alpine Rhine. Sooner or later all the streams in the country flow into the Rhine.
93677.m: Liechtenstein's debris flow streams drain into the Rhine.

93678.q: What are the barriers across a stream bed called that reduce the slope and slow down debris flows?
93678.e: Check dams are step-like walls made of concrete, wood or stone. They stop the stream from cutting deeper and carrying away more material.
93678.m: Check dams slow down water and rubble in the stream bed.

93679.q: Which plants help most on steep slopes to prevent debris flows?
a: The trees of a dense forest
93679.e: Tree roots hold the soil together, and the forest soaks up a lot of rainwater. As a result, less material is washed away.
93679.m: A dense forest protects slopes from debris flows.

93680.q: In which season do debris flows happen especially often in the Alps?
93680.e: In summer the ground has thawed and is free of snow, and short, heavy downpours are common. In the depths of winter the ground is frozen and covered with snow.
93680.m: Most debris flows in the Alps come down in summer.

93681.q: Why are debris flow streams often led through a village in concrete channels?
a: So that debris flows away quickly and in a controlled way
So that people can swim in them
So that fish can migrate better
So that the water gets warmer
93681.e: A smooth, wide channel leads the material along a fixed path through the village. This makes it less likely that the debris flow bursts its banks.
93681.m: Channels lead debris flows safely through villages.

93682.q: What does it mean when people are evacuated during a flood?
a: They are taken out of danger to safety
They have to pump out the water
They have to stay at home
93682.e: During the flood in August 2005, many people in Switzerland had to leave their homes. Rescue teams took them to safe places.
93682.m: To evacuate means to bring people to safety.

93683.q: What is a map called that shows where, for example, floods or avalanches threaten?
93683.e: After events like the 2005 flood, hazard maps became even more important. They show where you have to build carefully or take protective measures.
93683.m: Hazard maps show where natural hazards threaten.

93684.q: In which city did the Aare flood a whole old town district in August 2005?
93684.e: The Matte district in Bern lies right on the Aare below the old town. In August 2005 it was under water.
93684.m: In 2005, the Aare flooded a district of Bern.

93685.q: What is a debris flow, like the one that destroyed houses in Brienz in August 2005?
a: A stream of water, mud and stones
A strong wind in the valley
93685.e: In a debris flow, a stream carries along lots of mud, stones and wood. This mass is heavy and can destroy houses.
93685.m: A debris flow is a stream of water, mud and stones.

93686.q: Which river burst its banks near Bern and Thun in August 2005?
93686.e: After days of rain, the Aare rose sharply. It flooded parts of Bern and also Bern-Belp airport.
93686.m: In the 2005 flood, the Aare burst its banks.

93687.q: Which monastery and holiday village in Obwalden was cut off for days in August 2005?
93687.e: The Engelberger Aa destroyed the road and railway line into the valley. Engelberg could therefore only be reached by air.
93687.m: Engelberg was cut off after the 2005 flood.

93688.q: What was built in Thun after the 2005 flood to drain Lake Thun more quickly during floods?
93688.e: A flood relief tunnel carries extra water from Lake Thun into the Aare. This lets the lake level be lowered more quickly.
93688.m: A tunnel in Thun lowers the lake level during floods.

93689.q: What was the main cause of the August 2005 flood in Switzerland?
a: Several days of heavy rain on the northern side of the Alps
A dam bursting at the Grimsel lake
93689.e: A low-pressure area brought very large amounts of rain over several days. Streams and rivers burst their banks, and lakes rose sharply.
93689.m: Days of heavy rain caused the 2005 flood.

93690.q: What are the lattice-like steel frames on steep slopes called that stop snow from sliding?
93690.e: Snow bridges are put up in rows on steep slopes. They support the snow cover so that no avalanche breaks loose at all.
93690.m: Snow bridges support the snow cover on steep slopes.

93691.q: In which part of a slope are supporting structures against avalanches put up?
93691.e: Supporting structures are meant to stop an avalanche from starting at all. That is why they stand where avalanches typically break loose.
93691.m: Supporting structures stand where avalanches start.

a: A roof over a road that avalanches slide over
A viewing tower in a ski resort
93692.e: An avalanche gallery is a structure open at the side with a strong roof. The avalanche slides over it, while the traffic underneath stays protected.
93692.m: An avalanche slides over an avalanche gallery.

93693.q: What are snow fences on mountain ridges for?
a: They hold back snow blown by the wind
93693.e: The wind blows snow and piles it up behind ridges in dangerous cornices. Fences slow the wind so that the snow settles in a harmless place.
93693.m: Snow fences prevent dangerous build-ups of snow.

93694.q: What does a deflecting dam do with an avalanche?
a: It steers the avalanche past a village
It sets off the avalanche artificially
It measures the depth of the snow
93694.e: A deflecting dam is a bank built at an angle to the avalanche path. It guides the masses of snow in a harmless direction.
93694.m: Deflecting dams steer avalanches away from villages.

93695.q: Why are young trees often planted above avalanche barriers?
a: So that later a forest takes over the job
So that wood grows for stoves
So that the snow melts faster
93695.e: A healthy mountain forest also holds the snow cover in place. The barriers protect the young trees until the forest is big enough.
93695.m: Planting trees is meant to protect against avalanches in future.

93696.q: How do safety services set off avalanches in a controlled way before they come down uncontrolled?
93696.e: When avalanche danger is high, dangerous slopes are blasted on purpose. Pistes and roads are closed while this happens.
93696.m: Controlled blasting sets off avalanches safely.

93697.q: What is a catching dam in avalanche protection?
a: A bank that stops an avalanche
93697.e: A catching dam stands across the avalanche path. It slows the avalanche down and holds back the masses of snow before they reach the village.
93697.m: Catching dams stop avalanches before they reach villages.

93699.q: In which canton is the SLF (Institute for Snow and Avalanche Research)?
93699.e: The SLF is based in Davos in the canton of the Grisons. Davos lies at more than 1500 metres above sea level.
93699.m: The SLF is in the canton of the Grisons.

93700.q: WSL is the research institute that the SLF belongs to. Its letters come from German. What does the W stand for?
93700.e: WSL is the Swiss Federal Institute for Forest, Snow and Landscape Research. The SLF in Davos is one of its sites.
93700.m: The WSL researches forest, snow and landscape.

93701.q: What does the SLF publish every day in winter for the Swiss mountains?
93701.e: The avalanche bulletin shows how great the avalanche danger is in different areas. Anyone going off-piste should read it first.
93701.m: In winter, the SLF publishes the avalanche bulletin.

93702.q: How many danger levels does the avalanche warning in Switzerland have?
93702.e: The scale goes from level 1, low, to level 5, very high. It is the same throughout Europe.

93703.q: Which topic does the SLF also study besides snow and avalanches?
93703.e: The SLF also studies permanently frozen ground in the Alps. Thawing permafrost can lead to rockfalls.

93704.q: What does the SLF measure with its stations in the mountains to assess the avalanche danger?
a: The water level of the lakes
93704.e: Automatic stations constantly measure how much snow is lying, how strongly the wind is blowing and how warm it is. These values help with avalanche warnings.
93704.m: Snow depth, wind and temperature show the avalanche danger.

93705.q: What do SLF experts investigate after serious avalanche accidents?
a: How and why the avalanche came down
Who has to pay for the accident
What the weather will be like in summer
93705.e: The SLF writes expert reports on avalanche accidents. From these we learn how to prevent accidents better in future.
93705.m: The SLF looks into the causes of avalanche accidents.

93706.q: Which level of the avalanche danger scale is called “considerable”?
93706.e: The European scale has five levels, and “considerable” is right in the middle. At this level, avalanches can be triggered on many steep slopes even by a single person.

93707.q: What is the highest level of the avalanche danger scale called?
93707.e: Level 5 is called “very high”. Then many large avalanches can be expected, even on moderately steep ground.
93707.m: The highest avalanche danger level is called very high.

93708.q: When should you read the avalanche bulletin?
a: Before every trip away from the pistes
Only when the sun is shining
93708.e: The avalanche bulletin shows the current danger. Anyone going away from the secured pistes uses it to plan their trip in advance.
93708.m: Read the avalanche bulletin before every trip in the snow.

93709.q: Which colour is used for avalanche danger level 1, “low”?
93709.e: The levels are shown in colours from green through yellow and orange to red. Green stands for low danger.

93710.q: At which danger levels do most fatal avalanche accidents involving winter sports enthusiasts happen?
93710.e: At these middle levels, many people are out in the mountains, and the danger is often underestimated. When the danger is very high, most people stay at home.
93710.m: Never underestimate moderate and considerable avalanche danger.

93711.q: Which avalanche problem does the bulletin mention when the snow cover is soaked and weakened by warmth or rain?
93711.e: Water weakens the bonds between snow grains. That is why the danger of wet snow avalanches often rises during the day and in spring.
93711.m: Soaked snow leads to the avalanche problem wet snow.

93712.q: Besides the danger level, what information about the danger spots does the avalanche bulletin contain?
93712.e: The bulletin shows at which altitudes and on which slope directions the danger is especially high. This lets you avoid dangerous slopes.
93712.m: The bulletin gives the altitude and slope direction of the danger spots.

93713.q: From what steepness does a slope count as a steep slope in the avalanche bulletin?
93713.e: A slope steeper than about 30 degrees counts as a steep slope. From this steepness, slab avalanches can break loose.
93713.m: Steep slopes are steeper than about 30 degrees.

93714.q: What is a rockfall net on a rock face for?
a: It keeps birds away from the rock
93714.e: Rockfall nets are stretched between posts and the rock. They catch stones and boulders before they hit roads or houses.

93715.q: What material are modern rockfall nets usually made of?
93715.e: The nets are woven from very strong steel wire. They have to withstand enormous forces from falling boulders.
93715.m: Rockfall nets are made of high-strength steel wire.

93716.q: What else absorbs the force of a stone hitting a rockfall barrier?
93716.e: Braking elements are built into the supporting cables and change shape on impact. This slowly takes away the energy of the movement.
93716.m: Braking elements absorb the energy of the impact.

93717.q: In which unit is the impact energy a rockfall net can absorb given?
93717.e: The energy of a falling stone depends on its mass and speed. It is given in joules or kilojoules.
93717.m: The protective power of a net is measured in kilojoules.

93718.q: What has to happen to a protective net after a rockfall?
a: It has to be emptied and checked
It has to be painted again
It has to be taken down
93718.e: The stones it has caught put further strain on the net. Experts empty it and replace damaged parts.
93718.m: Full rockfall nets have to be emptied.

93719.q: What are the posts and cables of a rockfall net fixed to the slope with?
a: Anchors in the rock or ground
93719.e: Long anchors are drilled into the ground. They carry the forces into the ground when a stone hits.
93719.m: Anchors hold rockfall nets on the slope.

93720.q: What especially often loosens stones in the mountains, which then fall as rockfall?
a: Water freezing and thawing in cracks in the rock
93720.e: Water expands when it freezes and forces cracks in the rock open. When it thaws, stones can then fall out.
93720.m: Frost shattering loosens stones in the rock.

93721.q: Where in Switzerland do you often see rockfall nets?
a: Above roads and railway lines in mountain valleys
Above lakes on the Swiss Plateau
93721.e: On steep rock faces along transport routes there is often a danger of rockfall. Nets protect cars and trains there.
93721.m: Rockfall nets mainly protect transport routes.

93722.q: What does the colour blue mean on a Swiss hazard map?
93722.e: Blue marks areas with medium hazard. Building is only allowed there with conditions, for example with reinforced walls.
93722.m: On the hazard map, blue stands for medium danger.

93723.q: Which colour shows a low hazard on a Swiss hazard map?
93723.e: Yellow areas show a low hazard. People inside buildings are hardly at risk there, but damage to property is possible.
93723.m: On the hazard map, yellow means low danger.

93724.q: Who draws up the hazard maps for natural hazards in Switzerland?
93724.e: The cantons are responsible for the hazard maps, often working with specialist firms. The federal government supports them with guidelines and money.
93724.m: The cantons draw up the hazard maps.

93725.q: Which colour shows a considerable hazard on a Swiss hazard map, where you may not build new houses?
93725.e: Red areas are at high risk. Even people inside buildings are in danger there, so new building is not allowed.
93725.m: On the hazard map, red means considerable danger.

93726.q: What are hazard maps mainly used for in municipalities?
a: For planning where building is allowed
93726.e: Hazard maps feed into land-use planning and zoning plans. This avoids new houses in dangerous areas.
93726.m: Hazard maps help with planning where to build.

93727.q: What does a yellow and white striped area mean on a Swiss hazard map?
a: A remaining hazard from very rare events
93727.e: Yellow and white stripes show areas with a remaining hazard. These are events with a very low probability but possibly a big impact.
93727.m: Yellow and white stripes show a remaining hazard.

93728.q: Which two things are combined on a hazard map?
93728.e: The hazard level comes from how strong and how frequent an event is. A frequent, strong event gives the highest level.
93728.m: Hazard maps combine the strength and frequency of an event.

93729.q: What is the rougher overview map called that only shows where a natural hazard is possible?
93729.e: The hazard indication map shows over large areas where hazards could occur. The more detailed hazard map then grades the hazard.
93729.m: A hazard indication map shows possible hazard areas.

93730.q: Which karst cave on the north shore of Lake Thun can you visit?
93730.e: The St. Beatus Caves lie above Sundlauenen on Lake Thun. Part of the cave system is open to visitors.
93730.m: The St. Beatus Caves are on Lake Thun.

93731.q: Which substance in rainwater makes it able to dissolve limestone?
93731.e: Rainwater takes up carbon dioxide from the air and soil and forms carbonic acid. This slowly dissolves limestone.
93731.m: Carbonic acid in water dissolves limestone.

93732.q: Which large cave system in the Muota valley is one of the longest caves in Europe?
93732.e: The Hölloch in the canton of Schwyz has been surveyed at more than 200 kilometres long. It is the second-longest cave system in Europe (as of 2022).
93732.m: The Hölloch in the Muota valley is one of the longest caves in Europe.

93733.q: What are the dripstones hanging from the ceiling of a karst cave called?
93733.e: Stalactites grow downwards from the ceiling. Stalagmites grow upwards from the floor.
93733.m: Stalactites hang from the cave ceiling.

93734.q: What can form when water dissolves limestone underground over a long time?
93734.e: Water containing carbonic acid slowly dissolves limestone. Over thousands of years this creates cracks, passages and large caves.

93735.q: What often happens to rainwater in karst areas?
a: It seeps away and flows underground
93735.e: In karst areas there are few streams on the surface. The water disappears into cracks and comes out again at karst springs.
93735.m: In karst, water mostly flows underground.

93736.q: Why is drinking water from karst springs especially easy to pollute?
a: It flows fast and is hardly filtered
It contains a lot of salt
93736.e: In cracks and caves, water flows quickly without being filtered through fine layers of soil. Pollutants therefore reach the spring quickly.
93736.m: Karst water is hardly filtered and is sensitive.

93737.q: Which Swiss mountain range consists largely of limestone and has many karst features?
93737.e: The Jura is made mostly of limestone rocks. That is why there are many caves, sinkholes and karst springs there.
93737.m: The Jura is rich in karst features.

93738.q: How does a collapse sinkhole form?
a: The roof of a hollow space caves in
93738.e: Under the surface, water dissolves a hollow space. If the roof becomes too thin, it caves in and a funnel forms.
93738.m: A collapse sinkhole forms when a cave roof caves in.

93739.q: How does a solution sinkhole form?
a: The rock is slowly dissolved from above
The wind blows the sand away
93739.e: In places where a lot of water seeps in, the rock is dissolved more strongly. There the surface gradually sinks into a hollow.
93739.m: Solution sinkholes form slowly through dissolving.

93740.q: In which Swiss region are there especially many sinkholes?
93740.e: The Jura consists mainly of limestone, which water can dissolve. That is why there are very many sinkholes there.
93740.m: There are many sinkholes in the limestone mountains of the Jura.

93741.q: Apart from limestone, in which easily dissolved rock can sinkholes also form?
93741.e: Gypsum dissolves even more easily than limestone. In gypsum areas, sinkholes can therefore form especially quickly.

93742.q: Why can sinkholes be dangerous for houses and roads?
a: The ground can suddenly cave in
93742.e: There can be hollow spaces under a sinkhole. If it caves in, buildings or roads can sink.
93742.m: Above sinkholes, the ground can suddenly cave in.

93743.q: What is a hole called where a stream in karst suddenly disappears into the ground?
93743.e: In a swallow hole, also called a ponor, surface water sinks underground. It is often at the bottom of a sinkhole.
93743.m: In a swallow hole, water disappears into the karst.

93744.q: What does a sinkhole usually look like?
a: Like a funnel in the ground
93744.e: A sinkhole is a round hollow or funnel in the ground. It forms when water dissolves limestone or gypsum.
93744.m: A sinkhole is a funnel in the ground.

93745.q: Roughly how far did the mass of rock from Elm flow across the flat valley floor?
93745.e: After falling freely for several hundred metres, the rock spread out like a stream. It flowed about two kilometres down the valley.
93745.m: The mass of rock from Elm flowed about two kilometres.

93746.q: What is avalanche danger level 4 called?
93746.e: Level 4 is the second-highest level on the scale. Then large avalanches that start on their own are likely.
93746.m: Avalanche danger level 4 is called high.

a: A rock from which metal can be obtained profitably
A pure metal from the ground
93747.e: Ores contain metal compounds in such large amounts that mining them is worthwhile. The metal then has to be extracted chemically.

93748.q: Which ore is the most important raw material for producing aluminium?
93748.e: Bauxite contains a lot of aluminium oxide. First pure aluminium oxide is made from it, and this is then turned into aluminium.

93749.q: Which metal is obtained from haematite and magnetite?
93749.e: Haematite and magnetite are iron oxides. They are among the most important iron ores in the world.
93749.m: Haematite and magnetite are iron ores.

93750.q: What used to be mined at the Gonzen mine near Sargans?
93750.e: The Gonzen was one of the most important iron mines in Switzerland. Today you can visit it as a show mine.
93750.m: Iron ore was mined at the Gonzen near Sargans.

93751.q: Why does mined ore have to be processed first?
a: Because it contains a lot of worthless rock
93751.e: Ore is mixed in with worthless rock. During processing, it is separated from this as far as possible.
93751.m: Ore contains a lot of worthless rock.

93752.q: In what form are metals found in most ores?
a: As chemical compounds, such as oxides
As pure, shiny lumps of metal
93752.e: In nature, most metals are combined with oxygen or sulfur. Only a few, such as gold, are often found native, that is pure.
93752.m: Metals in ores are mostly found as compounds.

93753.q: Which metal is obtained from the ore chalcopyrite?
93753.e: Chalcopyrite is a compound of copper, iron and sulfur. It is the most important copper ore.

93754.q: What is mining ore in a huge open pit at the surface called?
93754.e: If the ore lies close to the surface, it is dug out in large pits. If it lies deep, tunnels are built underground.
93754.m: In open-cast mining, ore is dug out at the surface.

93755.q: How does the liquid iron get out of the blast furnace?
a: It flows out through a hole opened at the bottom
It is scooped out at the top
It is blown out as a powder
93755.e: A hole is opened at the bottom of the blast furnace. The glowing pig iron then flows out along channels. This is called tapping.
93755.m: The liquid iron flows out of the bottom of the blast furnace.

93756.q: Which substance serves as fuel and reducing agent in the blast furnace?
93756.e: Coke is almost pure carbon made from coal. It provides the heat and removes the oxygen from the iron ore.
93756.m: Coke heats the blast furnace and reduces the ore.

93758.q: Why is limestone added to the blast furnace?
a: It binds the waste rock into slag
93758.e: Limestone combines with the waste rock to form slag. This can easily be separated from the iron.
93758.m: Limestone helps remove the waste rock as slag.

93759.q: Why does the liquid slag float on top of the pig iron in the blast furnace?
a: It is hotter than the iron
93759.e: Slag is lighter than liquid iron. So it collects on top and can be drained off separately.
93759.m: Slag is lighter and floats on the iron.

93760.q: Roughly how much carbon does pig iron from the blast furnace contain?
93760.e: Pig iron takes up a lot of carbon in the blast furnace, around 4 per cent. That is why it is brittle and can hardly be forged.
93760.m: Pig iron contains around 4 per cent carbon.

93761.q: What is blown into the bottom of the blast furnace to make the fuel burn fiercely?
93761.e: Hot blast stoves heat air to over 1000 degrees. This hot air is blown into the bottom of the furnace as the “blast”.
93761.m: Hot air fans the fire in the blast furnace.

93762.q: Once it has been started, how long does a blast furnace usually run without a break?
93762.e: Ore, fuel and limestone are constantly filled in at the top, and liquid iron is taken out at the bottom. A blast furnace usually runs for many years until it has to be relined.
93762.m: A blast furnace runs for years without a break.

93763.q: At most, how much carbon does steel contain?
93763.e: Iron with at most about 2 per cent carbon counts as steel. More carbon makes the material brittle, like cast iron.
93763.m: Steel contains at most around 2 per cent carbon.

93764.q: What do you get if you remove a large part of the carbon from pig iron?
93764.e: Pig iron contains a lot of carbon and is brittle. If oxygen is blown onto it, carbon burns away and tough steel forms.
93764.m: Removing carbon turns pig iron into steel.

93765.q: Which metal mainly makes stainless steel rust-free?
93765.e: Stainless steel contains at least about 10.5 per cent chromium. The chromium forms a thin, protective oxide layer.

93766.q: What is steel in Switzerland mainly made from?
93766.e: Iron ore is no longer mined in Switzerland. Steelworks such as the one in Gerlafingen melt down scrap metal and make new steel from it.
93766.m: Swiss steel is made from scrap.

93767.q: How is scrap steel melted in an electric steelworks?
93767.e: Electric arcs with a very high temperature form between graphite electrodes and the scrap. These melt the scrap.
93767.m: Electric arc furnaces melt scrap with electricity.

93768.q: What happens to steel if you heat it strongly and then cool it quickly in water?
a: It becomes as soft as lead
93768.e: Rapid cooling, called quenching, changes the inner structure of the steel. It becomes harder. This process is called hardening.

93769.q: Why is steel an especially good material for recycling?
a: It can be melted down again without losing quality
It turns back into ore when it rusts
93769.e: Scrap steel can be melted down again and again and made into new steel. This saves ore and a lot of energy.
93769.m: Steel can be recycled again and again.

93770.q: What is the steel called that is placed inside concrete structures to make them strong under tension?
93770.e: Concrete copes well with pressure but cracks under tension. Steel bars placed inside, the reinforcement, take up the pulling forces.
93770.m: Reinforcing steel makes concrete strong under tension.

93771.q: Which metal is today obtained almost only by molten salt electrolysis?
93771.e: Aluminium is so reactive that it cannot be reduced with carbon. It is obtained with electricity from molten aluminium oxide.
93771.m: Aluminium is obtained by molten salt electrolysis.

93772.q: From which ore is aluminium obtained?
93772.e: Bauxite is a reddish rock with a lot of aluminium oxide. Pure aluminium oxide is obtained from it first, and then the metal is made using electricity.

93774.q: At which pole does the aluminium collect in molten salt electrolysis?
93774.e: Aluminium ions are positively charged. They move to the negative pole, the cathode, and become metal there.
93774.m: Aluminium forms at the negative pole.

93775.q: What are the anodes made of in aluminium electrolysis, which are slowly used up in the process?
93775.e: The carbon anodes react with the oxygen produced to form carbon dioxide. So they have to be replaced regularly.
93775.m: The carbon anodes burn away during electrolysis.

93776.q: Why does making new aluminium use so much energy?
a: The electrolysis needs a huge amount of electricity
Aluminium must be made in a vacuum
You need a lot of gold for it
93776.e: For one kilogram of aluminium, electrolysis needs over ten kilowatt hours of electricity. Recycling needs only a small part of that.
93776.m: New aluminium uses a huge amount of electricity.

93777.q: What does “molten salt” mean in the term molten salt electrolysis?
a: The substance is melted instead of dissolved in water
The metal is cooled with water
93777.e: In this electrolysis, the starting compound is melted. In a water solution, hydrogen would form instead of aluminium.
93777.m: In molten salt electrolysis, a melt is split up.

93778.q: Which metal is obtained by electrolysis of molten table salt?
93778.e: Table salt is sodium chloride. In the electrolysis of the melt, sodium forms at the negative pole and chlorine at the positive pole.
93778.m: Sodium is obtained from molten table salt.

93779.q: In which canton is Chippis, with its well-known aluminium works?
93779.e: Chippis lies near Sierre in the Rhône valley. The aluminium works have shaped the village for over a hundred years.
93779.m: The Chippis aluminium works are in Valais.

93780.q: From which raw material is aluminium obtained?
93780.e: Bauxite is a reddish rock with a lot of aluminium oxide. Aluminium is made from it in several steps.

93781.q: Why was an aluminium works built in a mountain valley in Valais, as at Chippis?
a: Because of water power for lots of electricity
Because of the many bauxite mines there
93781.e: Aluminium electrolysis needs an enormous amount of electricity. The mountain streams of Valais supplied it cheaply from water power.
93781.m: Water power made Valais attractive for aluminium works.

93782.q: Why is aluminium popular for vehicles and aircraft?
a: It is light and hardly corrodes
93782.e: Aluminium has a much lower density than steel. It also protects itself from corrosion with a thin oxide layer.
93782.m: Aluminium is light and hardly corrodes.

93783.q: Which process uses electric current to obtain aluminium?
93783.e: In electrolysis, electric current separates the aluminium from its compound. This needs a lot of electricity.

93784.q: Which things made of aluminium does almost every child know?
93784.e: Aluminium can easily be rolled into thin sheets and foils. Drinks cans and kitchen foil, for example, are made from it.
93784.m: Cans and kitchen foil are made of aluminium.

93785.q: Why is it especially worthwhile to recycle aluminium?
a: It needs much less energy than making it new
New aluminium can no longer be made
93785.e: Making it from bauxite needs an enormous amount of electricity. Melting down old aluminium saves most of this energy.
93785.m: Recycling aluminium saves a lot of energy.

93786.q: On which large river does Chippis lie?
93786.e: Chippis lies on the left bank of the Rhône. The Navisence from the Val d’Anniviers also flows into it there.

93787.q: What do you do when electroplating?
a: Coat an object with metal using electricity
93787.e: In electroplating, metal ions move from a solution onto the workpiece. There they form a thin layer of metal.

93788.q: In electroplating, which pole is the object to be coated connected to?
93788.e: The metal ions in the solution are positively charged. They are attracted by the negative pole and settle there as metal.
93788.m: In electroplating, the workpiece hangs on the negative pole.

93789.q: What do you absolutely need for electroplating?
93789.e: Only the current makes the metal ions move to the workpiece. There they settle as a thin layer of metal.
93789.m: Electroplating only works with electric current.

93790.q: What is electroplating with chromium called, for example on shiny taps?
93790.e: A layer of chromium is hard, shiny and resists corrosion. That is why many taps and fittings are chrome-plated.

93791.q: What must be dissolved in the liquid of an electroplating bath for a layer of silver to form?
93791.e: The solution contains a silver salt. The positively charged silver ions become silver metal on the workpiece.
93791.m: For a silver layer, the bath needs silver ions.

93792.q: In electroplating, what often happens to an anode made of the coating metal?
93792.e: At the positive pole, metal atoms go into solution as ions. This supplies the metal that settles on the workpiece.
93792.m: In electroplating, the metal anode supplies new ions.

93793.q: Why is cheap jewellery often gold-plated instead of made of pure gold?
a: A thin layer of gold is much cheaper
Gold is too light for jewellery
93793.e: In gold plating, only a wafer-thin layer of gold is applied. It looks like gold but uses very little of it.

93794.q: Apart from making things look nicer, what is electroplating often used for?
93794.e: A layer of metal can protect the base material from rust. Many screws, for example, are zinc-plated.
93794.m: Electroplated layers often protect against corrosion.

93795.q: Which energy conversion takes place in a battery when it powers a device?
93795.e: Chemical reactions take place in the battery in which electrons flow. This produces electric current.
93795.m: A battery turns chemical energy into electrical energy.

93796.q: Which Italian scientist built the first battery around 1800?
93796.e: Volta stacked zinc and copper discs with soaked cardboard in between. This voltaic pile was the first to supply a steady current.
93796.m: Alessandro Volta built the first battery around 1800.

93797.q: What voltage does an ordinary AA alkaline battery have?
93797.e: An alkaline manganese cell supplies 1.5 volts. For 9 volts, several cells are connected together in one block.

93798.q: Which rechargeable batteries are in most mobile phones and electric cars today?
93798.e: Lithium-ion batteries store a lot of energy for little weight. That is why they are used in mobile phones, laptops and electric cars.
93798.m: Mobile phones mostly run on lithium-ion batteries.

93799.q: What rule applies in Switzerland to shops that sell batteries?
a: They must take back used batteries free of charge
They may only sell rechargeable batteries
They must not take back batteries
93799.e: In Switzerland, shops are obliged to take batteries back. Disposal is paid for by an advance fee when you buy them.
93799.m: You take used batteries back to the shop.

93800.q: Why don’t old batteries belong in the household rubbish?
a: They contain pollutants and valuable metals
They are too heavy for the rubbish bag
They dissolve in the rubbish at once
They charge up again in the rubbish
93800.e: Batteries can contain poisonous substances that harm the environment. Also, metals such as zinc, nickel or lithium can be recovered.
93800.m: Batteries belong at the collection point.

93801.q: What is the battery pole called from which electrons flow into the circuit when it discharges?
93801.e: At the negative pole, electrons are released by the chemical reaction. They flow through the device to the positive pole.
93801.m: Electrons flow from the negative to the positive pole.

93802.q: Which two metals are often pushed into a lemon to build a lemon battery?
93802.e: You need two different metals as electrodes. Copper and zinc work well because they differ in how reactive they are.
93802.m: For a lemon battery you need copper and zinc.

93803.q: What does the lemon juice do in a lemon battery?
a: It conducts the ions as an electrolyte
It supplies all the energy as sugar
It insulates the metals from each other
93803.e: The sour juice contains dissolved ions and so completes the circuit inside the battery. Without an electrolyte, no current flows.
93803.m: The lemon juice acts as the electrolyte in the battery.

93804.q: Why does a light bulb usually not light up with a single lemon battery?
a: The voltage and current are too small
Lemon juice does not conduct electricity at all
93804.e: A lemon supplies just under 1 volt and only a very small current. That is not enough for a light bulb.
93804.m: A single lemon supplies too little current for a light bulb.

93805.q: How do you increase the voltage when you use several lemon batteries?
a: You put them in the fridge
93805.e: In a series circuit, the copper of one lemon is connected to the zinc of the next. The voltages add up.
93805.m: Lemons connected in series give more voltage.

93806.q: Which metal is the negative pole in a lemon battery?
93806.e: Zinc is more reactive than copper and gives up electrons more easily. It slowly dissolves and forms the negative pole.
93806.m: In a lemon battery, zinc is the negative pole.

93807.q: How many lemons of about 0.9 volts each do you need at least in series for 2.5 volts?
93807.e: Two lemons give 2 times 0.9 volts, so 1.8 volts, which is too little. Three lemons give 3 times 0.9 volts, so 2.7 volts.
93807.m: Three lemons in series supply about 2.7 volts.

93808.q: What can you use to check whether a lemon battery is supplying voltage?
93808.e: A voltmeter measures the electrical voltage between the two metals. You connect it to the copper and the zinc.
93808.m: A voltmeter measures the voltage of the lemon battery.

93809.q: With which other fruit or vegetable does this kind of battery also work?
93809.e: Potatoes and apples also contain water with dissolved ions. So they can serve as an electrolyte too.
93809.m: You can also build a battery with a potato.

93810.q: What makes a metal a precious metal?
a: It hardly reacts with air and water
It is as light as polystyrene
93810.e: Precious metals such as gold and platinum resist corrosion very well. They do not rust and keep their shine.
93810.m: Precious metals hardly react with air and water.

93811.q: Which of these metals is a precious metal?
93811.e: Platinum, like gold and silver, is a precious metal. Iron, aluminium and zinc are base metals.

93812.q: What is the chemical symbol for silver?
93812.e: The symbol Ag comes from the Latin word “argentum” for silver. Si stands for silicon.

93813.q: How much pure gold does 18-carat gold contain?
93813.e: Pure gold is 24 carat. 18 divided by 24 gives 0.75, so 75 per cent gold.
93813.m: 18 carat means three quarters pure gold.

93814.q: What role does Switzerland play in the world gold trade?
a: A large share of the gold is refined here
It has the biggest gold mines
Gold is made from lead here
93814.e: Several large gold refineries, mainly in Ticino, purify gold from all over the world. That makes Switzerland a centre of the gold trade.
93814.m: A lot of gold is refined in Switzerland.

93815.q: In which part of a car are precious metals such as palladium and rhodium used?
93815.e: In the catalytic converter, palladium and rhodium help turn poisonous exhaust gases into less harmful substances. They are not used up themselves.

93816.q: Which mixture of two acids can even dissolve gold?
93816.e: Aqua regia, or “royal water”, is a mixture of hydrochloric acid and nitric acid. It dissolves gold, which otherwise can hardly be attacked.

93817.q: Why does silver cutlery go dark over time?
a: It reacts with sulfur compounds in the air
It takes on colour from food
93817.e: Silver forms a dark layer of silver sulfide with sulfur compounds. This can be polished off again.
93817.m: Silver tarnishes because of sulfur compounds.

93818.q: Which two substances does iron need in order to rust?
93818.e: Iron only rusts when moisture and oxygen are both present. In dry air it hardly rusts.
93818.m: Iron rusts with water and oxygen.

93819.q: What is the greenish layer called that forms on copper roofs over time and protects the copper?
93819.e: Copper slowly reacts with substances in the air. This produces a green patina that protects the metal beneath.
93819.m: The green patina protects copper roofs.

93820.q: What is a sacrificial anode on a ship’s hull?
a: A piece of more reactive metal that corrodes instead of the hull
93820.e: A more reactive metal such as zinc or magnesium is connected to the steel hull. It dissolves first and so protects the steel.
93820.m: A sacrificial anode corrodes instead of the steel.

93821.q: What is a simple way to protect bare tools from rust?
a: With a thin film of oil
93821.e: A film of oil stops water and oxygen reaching the iron. That is why tools and bicycle chains are oiled.
93821.m: A film of oil protects iron from rust.

93822.q: Why doesn’t aluminium rust right through, even though it is a base metal?
a: A thin oxide layer protects it
Aluminium is always covered with paint
93822.e: In air, a thin, dense oxide layer forms on aluminium straight away. It protects the metal beneath from further corrosion.
93822.m: A thin oxide layer protects aluminium.

93823.q: Which simple method protects an iron garden gate from rust?
93823.e: The paint forms a layer that keeps water and oxygen away from the iron. If it is damaged, rust can form there.
93823.m: Anti-rust paint keeps water and oxygen away from iron.

93824.q: Why is rust on iron so harmful, while the layer on aluminium protects it?
a: Rust is loose and flakes off
93824.e: Rust is porous and lets water and air keep reaching the iron. So the corrosion eats deeper and deeper.
93824.m: Loose rust does not protect the iron.

a: The destruction of a metal by chemical reaction with its surroundings
The melting of a metal in a furnace
93825.e: Corrosion is a chemical reaction of the metal with substances from its surroundings, such as oxygen and water. Rusting is the corrosion of iron.
93825.m: Corrosion is chemical attack on metals.

a: Steel parts are dipped in liquid zinc
93826.e: The steel parts are dipped in a bath of molten zinc. Afterwards they are covered with a firm layer of zinc.
93826.m: In hot-dip galvanising, steel is dipped in liquid zinc.

93827.q: Roughly how hot is a zinc bath in hot-dip galvanising?
93827.e: Zinc melts at around 420 degrees. So the bath is kept at about 450 degrees.
93827.m: A zinc bath is around 450 degrees hot.

93828.q: Why does a zinc layer still protect the steel even when it is scratched?
a: Zinc is more reactive and corrodes first
93828.e: Zinc gives up electrons more easily than iron. So at a scratch the zinc corrodes first, and the steel next to it stays protected.
93828.m: Zinc protects steel even at scratches.

93829.q: Which parts along Swiss roads are typically hot-dip galvanised?
93829.e: Crash barriers stand outdoors all year and get splashed with salt water in winter. The zinc layer reliably protects them from rust.

93830.q: What is done to steel parts before hot-dip galvanising so that the zinc sticks well?
93830.e: In pickling, acid removes rust and scale from the surface. Zinc only bonds well to clean steel.
93830.m: Before galvanising, the steel is pickled.

93831.q: What forms at the boundary between steel and zinc in hot-dip galvanising?
93831.e: In the hot bath, iron and zinc combine at the surface. This makes the layer stick very firmly to the steel.
93831.m: Hot-dip galvanising forms an iron-zinc alloy.

93832.q: What does freshly hot-dip galvanised steel often look like?
a: Shiny silver with a crystal pattern
93832.e: The zinc layer shines silver and often shows a pattern of zinc crystals. Over time it turns dull grey.

93833.q: Which large pharmaceutical company has its headquarters in Basel?
93833.e: Novartis is one of the largest pharmaceutical companies in the world and is based in Basel. Nestlé is based in Vevey, Swatch in Biel and Swisscom in Bern.
93833.m: Novartis has its headquarters in Basel.

93834.q: What happened on 1 November 1986 at Schweizerhalle near Basel?
a: A chemical warehouse burnt down and poisoned the Rhine
A nuclear power station was opened
A new bridge over the Rhine collapsed
93834.e: When a Sandoz warehouse caught fire, firefighting water carrying chemicals flowed into the river. Fish and other animals died along many kilometres.
93834.m: The Schweizerhalle fire in 1986 caused a huge fish kill.

93835.q: What do the Basel companies Roche and Novartis mainly make?
93835.e: Roche and Novartis are among the largest pharmaceutical companies in the world. They develop and sell medicines.
93835.m: Basel is a centre of the pharmaceutical industry.

93836.q: Which river was important to Basel’s chemical industry as a transport route and water source?
93836.e: Raw materials could be delivered by ship along the Rhine. The factories also needed a lot of water.
93836.m: The Rhine was central to Basel’s chemical industry.

93837.q: What was DDT, discovered in Basel, used for?
93837.e: In 1939 it was discovered in Basel that DDT kills insects. Later it was banned in many countries because of the harm it does to the environment.

93838.q: What does the Basel company Syngenta mainly make?
93838.e: Syngenta is an agrochemical company. It sells products against pests and seeds for farming.

93839.q: Which building in Basel, at 205 metres, is the tallest in Switzerland (as of 2025)?
93839.e: The Roche Tower Building 2 was completed in 2022 and is 205 metres tall. It towers over the neighbouring Building 1, which is 178 metres.
93839.m: Switzerland’s tallest tower belongs to Roche in Basel.

93840.q: How long does hot-dip galvanising typically protect steel outdoors?
93840.e: The zinc layer wears away only very slowly. Depending on the surroundings, the protection often lasts from 25 to over 50 years.
93840.m: Hot-dip galvanising protects steel for decades.

93841.q: What does the figure 999.9 on a gold bar mean?
a: It is 999.9 parts per thousand gold
It was made in the year 999
93841.e: The number gives the purity in thousandths. 999.9 means almost pure gold.
93841.m: A bar marked 999.9 is almost pure gold.

93842.q: What did many Basel chemical companies start out making in the 19th century?
93842.e: Basel’s silk ribbon industry needed a lot of colours. So the first chemical companies made artificial dyes.
93842.m: Basel’s chemical industry began with dyes.

93843.q: What is slag from the blast furnace often used for afterwards?
a: As a building material, for example for cement
93843.e: Cooled blast furnace slag is a stone-like material. It is used in road building and to make cement.
93843.m: Blast furnace slag is used as a building material.

93844.q: Why must a workpiece be thoroughly cleaned and degreased before electroplating?
a: So that the metal layer sticks well
93844.e: Grease and dirt stop the metal settling directly on the surface. Otherwise the layer flakes off later.
93844.m: An electroplated layer only sticks to clean surfaces.

93845.q: In what form is data sent through a fibre optic cable?
93845.e: In an optical fibre, data is sent as very fast pulses of light. A light signal can stand for a 1, for example, and no light for a 0.
93845.m: Fibre optic cables send data with light.

93846.q: Which physical effect traps the light inside an optical fibre?
93846.e: If the light hits the boundary between two layers of glass at a shallow enough angle, it is completely reflected back. This guides the light even round bends.
93846.m: Total internal reflection keeps the light trapped in the optical fibre.

93847.q: What is the innermost part of an optical fibre called, where the light travels?
93847.e: An optical fibre consists of a thin core and a cladding around it. The core has a higher refractive index than the cladding, so the light stays in the core.
93847.m: The light travels in the core of the fibre, and the cladding surrounds it.

93848.q: What raw material is the glass for optical fibres mainly made from?
93848.e: Optical fibres for data lines are made of very pure quartz glass, that is silicon dioxide. This glass is so clear that light can travel many kilometres.
93848.m: Optical fibres are made of very pure quartz glass.

93849.q: What advantage does a fibre optic cable have over a copper cable?
a: It is not affected by electrical interference
93849.e: Light in glass is not disturbed by electric and magnetic fields. In addition, an optical fibre can carry much more data over longer distances.
93849.m: Fibre optics are fast and unaffected by electrical interference.

93850.q: Why is the internet faster when the optical fibre goes all the way into the flat?
a: The data doesn't have to travel over old copper lines
The flat is then closer to the satellite
93850.e: Optical fibre can carry much more data than a copper cable. If it goes all the way into the flat, there is no slow copper section left.
93850.m: Fibre right into the flat makes the internet fast.

93851.q: How do fibre optic cables mainly connect the continents for the internet?
a: As undersea cables on the seabed
93851.e: By far the largest part of international data traffic runs through undersea cables with optical fibres on the seabed. Satellites only carry a small part.
93851.m: Undersea fibre optic cables connect the continents.

93852.q: Roughly how thin is a single optical fibre?
a: About as thin as a hair
About as thick as a pencil
About as thick as a garden hose
About as thick as an arm
93852.e: An optical fibre is about a tenth of a millimetre thick. A cable often contains many such fibres in a protective sheath.
93852.m: An optical fibre is as thin as a hair.

93853.q: What kind of light is mostly used in fibre optic networks?
93853.e: Data networks mostly use infrared light with wavelengths of around 1300 or 1550 nanometres. In these ranges the light is weakened especially little in the glass.
93853.m: Fibre optic networks mostly use invisible infrared light.

93854.q: What does roaming mean for mobile phones?
a: The phone uses another network abroad
The phone switches to flight mode
93854.e: Abroad your own provider's network is usually not available. When roaming, the phone logs into a partner network, which often costs extra.
93854.m: When roaming, the phone uses a partner network abroad.

93855.q: Which emergency number works all over Europe, including from a mobile phone?
93855.e: 112 is the standard European emergency number and works in all EU countries and in Switzerland. In Switzerland there are also 117 (police), 118 (fire brigade) and 144 (ambulance).
93855.m: The emergency number 112 works all over Europe.

93856.q: What happens during a so-called handover while you are on the phone in a moving train?
a: The call is passed on to the next radio cell
The phone switches to a landline
93856.e: When you move, the network passes the connection from one radio cell to the next. Ideally, the call does not drop.
93856.m: During a handover the connection moves from cell to cell.

93857.q: What does the abbreviation SIM stand for in SIM card?
93857.e: The SIM card is the “Subscriber Identity Module”. It identifies the phone on the network as a customer of a particular provider.
93857.m: The SIM card identifies you on the mobile network.

93858.q: With which 2nd-generation mobile standard was the text message (SMS) introduced?
93858.e: GSM is the standard of the second mobile generation (2G). It brought digital calls and the short text message, SMS.
93858.m: Text messages came with the digital GSM network.

93859.q: What did the first text message, sent in 1992, say?
93859.e: On 3 December 1992 the engineer Neil Papworth sent the message “Merry Christmas” from a computer to a mobile phone. This is considered the first text message.
93859.m: The first text message wished people a merry Christmas in 1992.

93860.e: LTE stands for “Long Term Evolution” and is the fourth mobile generation. Above all it brought much faster mobile internet.

93861.q: What is the aerial site called through which mobile phones are connected to the mobile network?
93861.e: A base station consists of aerials and equipment that talk by radio to the phones in its cell. From there the data usually travels on by cable.
93861.m: Mobile phones send signals to the nearest base station.

93863.q: What does the “G” in the name 5G stand for?
93863.e: 5G is the fifth generation of mobile communications. Each new generation has so far mainly brought faster data transmission.

93864.q: What does very low latency, which 5G is supposed to make possible, mean?
a: Data arrives with very little delay
More photos fit on the phone
93864.e: Latency is the delay before data reaches its destination. 5G is meant to cut it to a few milliseconds, which is important for remote-controlled machines, for example.
93864.m: Low latency means a short delay.

93865.q: Why do 5G signals with very high frequencies (millimetre waves) only reach a short distance?
a: They are strongly weakened by obstacles
93865.e: Very high frequencies are strongly weakened by walls, trees and even rain. That is why you need lots of small aerials close together for them.
93865.m: The higher the frequency, the shorter the range usually is.

93866.q: What can a modern 5G aerial do so that less energy is lost?
a: Direct the signal towards the phone
93866.e: Modern 5G aerials have many small aerial elements. With them they direct the radio signal like a beam of light towards the device.
93866.m: 5G aerials can direct the signal towards the device.

93867.q: What did the mobile phone companies buy at auction from the federal government in 2019 so that they could offer 5G?
93867.e: Every mobile network needs certain radio frequencies. Switzerland auctioned the frequencies for 5G to the mobile phone companies in 2019.

93868.q: What does Switzerland set for mobile phone aerials to protect people?
a: The number of phones per family
93868.e: A federal ordinance sets limits for the radiation from aerials. Especially strict values apply where people spend a long time.
93868.m: Strict radiation limits apply to mobile phone aerials in Switzerland.

93869.q: What is meant by the “Internet of Things”, which 5G is supposed to promote?
a: Many devices and sensors are connected to the internet
You only buy things on the internet
The internet is printed on paper
93869.e: In the Internet of Things, everyday objects such as sensors, meters or machines are networked. 5G can serve a great many such devices at the same time in one radio cell.
93869.m: In the Internet of Things many objects are networked.

93870.q: What kind of radiation does 5G use for transmission?
93870.e: Like all mobile networks, 5G transmits with electromagnetic waves in the radio frequency range. This radiation is non-ionising, so it cannot ionise atoms.

93871.q: What is the main job of a transmitting aerial?
a: Converting electrical signals into radio waves
93871.e: A transmitting aerial sends out electrical oscillations as electromagnetic waves. A receiving aerial does the opposite and turns radio waves back into electrical signals.
93871.m: Aerials turn electrical signals into radio waves and back.

93873.q: What do you need a satellite dish, which looks like a bowl, for?
93873.e: The curved dish focuses the weak signals of a satellite onto one point. That is where the receiver head sits, which picks up the signals.
93873.m: A satellite dish focuses satellite signals onto one point.

93874.q: How long is the wavelength of a radio wave at 100 megahertz (speed of light about 300,000 km/s)?
93874.e: Wavelength equals the speed of light divided by the frequency: 300,000,000 m/s divided by 100,000,000 Hz gives 3 m.
93874.m: The wavelength is the speed of light divided by the frequency.

93875.q: How is the size of an aerial usually related to the frequency?
a: The higher the frequency, the smaller the aerial
The higher the frequency, the bigger the aerial
93875.e: Aerials are often as long as a fraction of the wavelength, for example half a wavelength. High frequencies have short waves, which is why mobile phone aerials are so small.

93877.q: Why are transmitting aerials often placed on tall towers or mountains?
a: So that the radio waves reach further
So that they use less electricity
So that birds don't disturb them
So that they stay cool in summer
93877.e: Radio waves are blocked by hills and buildings. From a high place they reach a much larger area.
93877.m: High up, radio waves reach further.

93878.q: Why do television aerials on the roof point in a particular direction?
a: Because they receive best from the direction of the transmitter
Because the wind turns them that way
Because all aerials must point north
93878.e: Such roof aerials have several parallel rods. These focus the reception in one direction, so they are pointed at the transmitter.
93878.m: Roof aerials are pointed at the transmitter.

93879.q: Who is the wireless technology Bluetooth named after?
93879.e: The name recalls the Viking king Harald Bluetooth, who united parts of Denmark and Norway in the 10th century. Just as he brought peoples together, Bluetooth is meant to connect devices.
93879.m: Bluetooth is named after King Harald Bluetooth.

93880.q: What is the Bluetooth logo made of?
93880.e: The logo combines the Nordic runes for H and B, the initials of Harald Blåtand. That is why it looks like a pointed B.
93880.m: The Bluetooth logo combines the runes H and B.

93881.q: What kind of connection is Bluetooth mainly intended for?
93881.e: Bluetooth connects devices nearby, such as headphones, keyboards or speakers. Typical ranges are about 10 metres, or more depending on the device.
93881.m: Bluetooth connects devices over short distances.

93882.q: Which other wireless network at home uses similar frequencies to Bluetooth?
